Photo: Leviosa Hou / Unsplash
Topic 01 — Precompetition Nutrition

Glycogen Is the Fuel at Stake

Storage Capacity
~15 g glycogen per kg body weight, liver + muscle. An 80 kg athlete stores ~1,200 g.
Main fuel for high-intensity exercise (>70% VO2max) → depletion = muscular fatigue.
High or low glycemic index carbs before competition — no proven advantage either way; choose by individual tolerance and fiber content.
Topic 01 — Precompetition Nutrition

Timing Framework

Timing before eventCarbohydrateProtein
4+ hours1–4 g/kg body weight0.15–0.25 g/kg body weight
2 hours~1 g/kg body weight—
~1 hourLiquid carbs / gels / gummies preferred (empty stomach faster)—
Closer to competition → smaller quantities, more liquid-based carbohydrate sources.
Topic 01 — Precompetition Nutrition

Avoiding GI Distress

  • AvoidHigh-fat + high-fiber foods → slow digestion → cramps mid-exercise
  • AvoidSugar alcohols (sorbitol, mannitol) → gas, bloating, laxative effect
  • WatchHigh-fructose, high-FODMAP foods → increased GI distress risk
  • DoTrial all precompetition foods in practice first — never on game day
Topic 01 — Precompetition Nutrition

Aerobic Endurance: Overnight-Fast Risk

The Problem
Morning starts after overnight fast → low blood sugar + depleted liver glycogen before the gun even fires.
The Fix
Carbs consumed 3+ hours before competition significantly improve glycogen stores and time to exhaustion.
Crossover study: high-CHO meal alone → +9% endurance capacity vs. placebo. Meal + CHO-electrolyte drink during exercise → +22%.
Topic 02

Carbohydrate
Loading

Topic 02 — Carbohydrate Loading

Why Load Carbohydrate?

Muscle + liver glycogen depletion→Fatigue in long-duration exercise→Carb loading maximizes stores beforehand
Benefits events >90 minutes — distance runners, road cyclists, cross-country skiers, and other glycogen-depletion-risk athletes.
Photo: Adelio / Unsplash
Topic 02 — Carbohydrate Loading

Two Loading Protocols

Standard Protocol
3 days high-CHO diet + tapering exercise the week before + full rest day before event.
8–10 g CHO/kg body weight/day → 20–40% increase in muscle glycogen above normal.
Marathon Protocol
Higher intake suggested for runners in the 36–48 hours before a marathon.
10–12 g CHO/kg body weight over the 36–48 h window.
Topic 02 — Carbohydrate Loading

Sex Differences: A Calorie Problem

Early studies showed weaker carb-loading response in women — but the real issue was inadequate total daily calorie intake, not sex.
The Fix
Women who habitually eat <2,400 kcal/day struggle to add enough carbohydrate on top of a low base intake.
Raising total energy intake above 2,400 kcal alongside a higher-CHO diet restores the glycogen-storage benefit.
Menstrual Cycle Note
Glycogen storage capacity is naturally greater in the luteal phase vs. early follicular phase.
Carbohydrate loading + increased intake can compensate for this difference at any cycle phase.
Photo: embrace comfort / Unsplash
Topic 02 — Carbohydrate Loading

Practical Considerations

  • WatchOligosaccharides (beans, peas, onions, inulin-added bars) → rapid fermentation → gas + bloating
  • WatchTemporary weight gain from water bound to stored glycogen — expect and rehearse this in practice
  • IndividualBenefit magnitude varies athlete to athlete — always trial before competition day

Carb loading works — but only at 8–10 g/kg/day. Below that threshold, athletes see none of the glycogen-storage benefit.

Topic 03

During-Event

Topic 03 — During-Event Nutrition

The Sport Drink Formula

Sodium
20–30 mEq/L
(460–690 mg with chloride)
Potassium
2–5 mEq/L
(78–195 mg)
Carbohydrate
5–10% concentration
(6–8% ideal — >8% delays gastric emptying)
Hydrate hours before exercise for fluid absorption + urine output. Limit in-exercise water weight loss to <2% body weight.
Photo: Adelio / Unsplash
Topic 03 — During-Event Nutrition

Aerobic Endurance: Carb Intake Rate

28–144 g/hour of mixed carbohydrate (sucrose + fructose + glucose/maltodextrin) extends time to exhaustion and improves performance.
Oxidation Ceiling
Exogenous CHO oxidation caps at ~1.0–1.1 g/min regardless of higher intake — limited by gut absorption + delivery rate.
Multi-Transportable Carbs
Combining sugar types (each with its own intestinal transporter) raises total absorption + oxidation vs. a single sugar type.
Topic 03 — During-Event Nutrition

Intermittent Sports: Soccer, Tennis, Team Play

The Challenge
A tennis match can run 4 hours — longer than most aerobic endurance events — with fluid loss exceeding 2.5 L/hour.
Athletes can't drink continuously → recommended 200–400 mL per changeover.
Performance Effect
CHO supplementation may not change perceived exertion, but improves stroke quality — velocity, precision, error rate — during prolonged play.
Topic 03 — During-Event Nutrition

Two Extra Levers

  • CNS EffectRinsing carbohydrate through the mouth (no ingestion) improves ~1-hour performance by 2–3%
  • MixedAdding protein to a carbohydrate gel: helps time-to-exhaustion, no clear benefit in time-trial studies

During-event fueling is about a steady carbohydrate stream plus staying under 2% body-weight fluid loss — not maximum intake.

Photo: Sebastian Laverde / Unsplash
Topic 04

Postcompetition
Nutrition

Topic 04 — Postcompetition Nutrition

Glycogen Resynthesis: Two Phases

Phase 1 — Fast
Insulin-independent. Lasts 30–60 minutes. Rapid glycogen synthesis.
Phase 2 — Slow
Insulin-dependent. Lasts several hours. Much slower synthesis rate.
Rapid resynthesis needs 1.0–1.85 g CHO/kg/hour immediately after exercise, repeated every 15–60 min for up to 5 hours.
Topic 04 — Postcompetition Nutrition

Does Timing Actually Matter?

Recovery windowStrategy
>24 hours to recoverTotal daily carbohydrate matters more than immediate timing — glycogen fully restores over 24 h
<24 hours to recoverEat/drink high-CHO immediately + at regular intervals to accelerate resynthesis
Marathon / muscle-damaging eventsResynthesis delayed even with adequate CHO — mechanical/metabolic muscle damage
Photo: Lukas Blazek / Unsplash
Topic 04 — Postcompetition Nutrition

Why Protein After Training

Muscle Repair
Starts building/repair, may reduce postevent soreness after prolonged aerobic endurance exercise.
Glycogen Bonus
If CHO intake is below 1.2 g/kg/hour, added protein increases the rate of glycogen storage.
Dose
At least 20–40 g high-quality protein within a 2-hour window after aerobic endurance exercise.
Photo: Lukas Blazek / Unsplash
Topic 04 — Postcompetition Nutrition

Strength/Power: Restoring Glycogen Fast

Single resistance-training bout depleted glycogen by ~29% after 6 sets to failure.
With Carbohydrate
1.5 g CHO/kg immediately + again 1 h later → glycogen restored to 91% of preexercise levels within 6 hours.
Water Only
Same timeline, water only → glycogen restored to just 75% of preexercise levels.
Protein dose: 20–50 g (8.5–20 g essential amino acids) high-leucine protein in younger adults; 40 g+ in older adults, to maximally stimulate muscle protein synthesis.
Topic 04 — Postcompetition Nutrition

Daily Protein: Distribution Beats a Single Dose

Resistance training raises muscle sensitivity to amino acids for 24–48 hours — but a single meal's anabolic window lasts only 3–5 hours.
20–40 g protein every 3–4 hours is the practical strategy for meeting daily targets and sustaining muscle remodeling.

Four Training Goals

2

4

Topic 05 — Nutrition for Various Performance Goals

Macronutrient Targets by Goal

GoalCarbohydrateProtein (g/kg/day)
Aerobic Endurance8–10 g/kg during demanding phases1.4–2.0
Strength/Speed5–6 g/kg during peak training1.4–2.0

Photo: John Arano / Unsplash
Topic 05 — Nutrition for Various Performance Goals

Sport-Specific Protein Snapshot

Endurance
1.4–2.0 g/kg/day. Higher-leucine, fast protein post-session; distributed every 3–4 h.
Team/Intermittent
Higher-protein day-of during heavy travel/tournament schedules; protein post-game to offset muscle damage.
Weight-Class Sports
Higher relative protein (g/kg) during energy restriction to preserve lean mass while cutting.
Topic 05 — Nutrition for Various Performance Goals

One Consistent Pattern

Across every goal: protein spread across the day (every 3–4 h) outperforms a single large postworkout dose.

Match carbohydrate to training demand, protein to recovery need.

Topic 06

Estimating
Calorie Needs

Topic 06 — Estimating Calorie Needs

BMR vs. RMR

Basal Metabolic Rate
Measured after 12–14 h fast, resting supine, motionless, awake. The stricter, lower measure.
Resting Metabolic Rate
Easier to measure (no overnight fast needed) — runs 10–20% higher than BMR due to recent food/activity.
Fat-free mass explains 70–80% of the individual variation in RMR.
Topic 06 — Estimating Calorie Needs

Three Components of Daily Energy Expenditure

BMR
65–70%
Physical Activity
20–30%
Thermic Effect of Food
10–15%
Physical activity is the most variable component — it rises with training frequency, intensity, duration, and non-training daily activity.
Topic 06 — Estimating Calorie Needs

The Cunningham Equation

”

RMR = 500 + 22 × (FFM in kg)

Unlike IOM prediction equations, Cunningham accounts for fat-free mass directly — making it more applicable to athletes with above-average muscle mass.

Apply an activity factor (1.2 sedentary → 1.9 heavy activity) to RMR, or use MET values for activity-specific caloric cost.
Topic 06 — Estimating Calorie Needs

Physical Activity Level Coefficients

PAL categoryDescriptionCoefficient (M/F)
SedentaryCommon activities of daily living (ADLs)1.00 / 1.00
Low activeADLs + 30–60 min moderate activity daily1.12 / 1.19
ActiveADLs + ≥1 h moderate activity daily1.25 / 1.27
Very activeADLs + ≥1 h moderate + 1 h vigorous (or 2 h moderate)1.45 / 1.48

Calorie needs = RMR × PAL coefficient — a starting estimate, not a fixed prescription.

Topic 07

Weight Gain
Strategies

Topic 07 — Weight Gain Strategies

The Core Numbers

Calorie Surplus
~500 additional calories per day — enough to gain weight without excess fat, adjusted per athlete.
Protein Target
1.6–2.2 g/kg body weight/day to maximize lean mass gains.
Photo: Sven Mieke / Unsplash
Topic 07 — Weight Gain Strategies

Protein Level Decides Where Calories Go

8-week controlled overfeeding study, 16 adults, low (5%) vs. normal/high (15–25%) protein diets.
Normal/High Protein
Stored ~45% of excess calories as lean body mass.
Low Protein
Stored ~95% of excess calories as body fat.
Topic 07 — Weight Gain Strategies

Two Force Multipliers

Creatine Monohydrate
Safely and effectively increases lean body weight — worth adding for athletes pursuing mass gain.
Nutrition Counseling
21 elite athletes: counseled group had greater lean mass gains at 8–12 weeks — and benefits persisted 12 months later.
Topic 08

Weight (Fat) Loss
& Body Composition

Topic 08 — Weight (Fat) Loss & Body Composition

What Actually Predicts Success?

Low-carb vs. low-fat: no difference in weight loss when calories are equally restricted. Diet type doesn't decide the outcome.
The Two Real Predictors
Total calorie intake + dietary adherence — the ability to sustain the plan over time.
Protect Lean Mass
1.8–2.7 g protein/kg/day (≈2.3–3.1 g/kg fat-free mass) + a moderate ~500 kcal/day deficit.
Photo: Towfiqu barbhuiya / Unsplash
Topic 08 — Weight (Fat) Loss & Body Composition

BMI Classification & Disease Risk

CategoryBMI (kg/m²)Disease risk
Underweight<18.5—
Normal18.5–24.9—
Overweight25.0–29.9Increased–High
Obesity I30.0–34.9High–Very High
Obesity II35.0–39.9Very High
Extreme Obesity≥40Extremely High
BMI can't distinguish fat from muscle — overestimates body fat in muscular athletes, underestimates it in those who've lost muscle mass.
Topic 08 — Weight (Fat) Loss & Body Composition

Rapid Weight Loss: Red Flags

  • RiskVoluntary dehydration — diuretics, sauna, water/salt manipulation, layered clothing
  • RiskFasting, fad diets, excessive spitting
  • RiskSelf-induced vomiting, laxative abuse, thermogenic-aid misuse
Common in weight-class or judged sports: wrestling, boxing, lightweight crew, weightlifting, gymnastics.
Topic 08 — Weight (Fat) Loss & Body Composition

The Cost of Cutting Too Fast

Physical
Dehydration, heat illness, cramping, reduced strength, low blood pressure, electrolyte imbalance, kidney failure.
Performance & Safety
Lean mass loss, fatigue, dizziness, suppressed immunity, hormone imbalance — training and performance both put at risk.

The S&C professional's role: recognize the warning signs, document concerns, and loop in medical/dietetic support.

Topic 09

Relative Energy
Deficiency in
Sport (RED-S)

Topic 09 — Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (RED-S)

Low Energy Availability (LEA)

”

Energy Availability (EA) = Energy Intake − Exercise Energy Expenditure, relative to fat-free mass (FFM).

RED-S is the collection of physiological dysfunctions that follow sustained LEA — affecting metabolic rate, menstrual function, bone health, immunity, and cardiovascular health.

First recognized in the 2014 international RED-S consensus statement.
Photo: Stacey Koenitz / Unsplash
Topic 09 — Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (RED-S)

Where the Line Sits

Optimal EA
~45 kcal/kg FFM/day
Severe Perturbation
<30 kcal/kg FFM/day
Male athletes appear more physiologically resilient at low EA than female athletes, though not immune.
Topic 09 — Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (RED-S)

What LEA Disrupts

Endocrine & Menstrual
Disrupts hormonal balance via the HPG axis → amenorrhea, oligomenorrhea in female athletes.
Bone & Metabolic
↓ bone mineral density, ↑ bone stress injury risk; ↓ RMR; iron deficiency.
Immune & Psychological
Impaired immunity, GI/cardiovascular effects; ↑ depression, eating disorder, and stress-management risk.
Topic 09 — Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (RED-S)

Injury Risk & Performance Cost

LEA may be one of the strongest predictors of injury risk in athletes.
Performance impact is often indirect: impaired fuel storage/use, reduced training volume, and higher illness risk — direct evidence is still limited.
Photo: Omar Ramadan / Unsplash

Feeding and

Topic 10 — Feeding and Eating Disorders

Four Categories to Recognize

1
Anorexia Nervosa
Restriction + intense fear of weight gain
2
Binge-Eating Disorder
Uncontrolled binges, no purging
3
Bulimia Nervosa
Binge-purge cycle
4
ARFID, Pica, Rumination
Less common feeding disturbances
Topic 10 — Feeding and Eating Disorders · 1 of 4

Anorexia Nervosa — Restriction & Fear

What It Is
Distorted body image + intense fear of weight gain → excessive calorie restriction, severe weight loss. Ritualistic behaviors: repeated weighing, cutting food small, careful portioning.
Two Subtypes
Restricting type — no regular binge/purge. Binge-eating/purging type — regularly binges or purges.
Prevalence & Severity
Peaks early 20s. Lifetime prevalence (ages 10–39): 0.21–0.89% females, 0.19–0.67% males. Only 14% of females and 28.2% of males seek treatment. Highest mortality rate of any mental health disorder.
Topic 10 — Feeding and Eating Disorders · 2 of 4

Binge-Eating Disorder

Diagnostic Pattern
Uncontrolled binge episodes ≥1×/week for 3 weeks, with ≥3 of: eating rapidly, eating past fullness, eating without hunger, eating alone from embarrassment, guilt/disgust afterward.
Key Distinction
No purging (unlike bulimia) → often associated with overweight/obesity, including morbid obesity (BMI >40).
Lifetime prevalence: 0.69–1.93% males, 1.08–3.14% females. Peak onset early-to-mid 20s. ~30% receive treatment.
Topic 10 — Feeding and Eating Disorders · 3 of 4

Bulimia Nervosa

Diagnostic Pattern
Recurrent binges of objectively large amounts, followed by purging (vomiting, intense exercise, laxatives, diuretics). Binge-purge cycle ≥1×/week for 3 months.
Key Distinction
More likely normal weight (not underweight) — but unhappy with weight/body, fears weight gain, feels loss of control during binges.
Average onset early 20s. Lifetime prevalence: 0.08–0.30% males, 0.56–1.7% females. ~16–18% receive treatment.
Topic 10 — Feeding and Eating Disorders · 4 of 4

Less-Common Feeding Disturbances

ARFID
Avoidance/lack of interest in food (not body-image driven) → significant weight loss, nutritional deficiency, or reliance on supplements/enteral feeding.
Pica
Eating nonnutritive substances (clay, ice, hair, chalk) for ≥1 month. Linked to iron deficiency — test for anemia.
Rumination Disorder
Chewing, reswallowing, or spitting regurgitated food for ≥1 month, unrelated to a medical condition.
Topic 10 — Feeding and Eating Disorders

Signs to Watch For

Anorexia — Consequences
Osteopenia/osteoporosis, mild anemia, muscle wasting, delayed puberty, low blood pressure, slowed heart rate, infertility, organ damage.
Bulimia — Consequences
Inflamed throat, swollen salivary glands, worn tooth enamel, acid reflux, intestinal distress, severe dehydration, electrolyte imbalance.
Abnormal eating patterns or amenorrhea alone are not diagnostic — a qualified professional must confirm any diagnosis.
Topic 10 — Feeding and Eating Disorders

Refer — Don't Diagnose or Treat

  • RoleRecognize signs & symptoms; know the referral network before you need it
  • RoleConnect athletes to a qualified physician + treatment team for diagnosis and care
  • Not Your RoleDiagnosing or treating the disorder yourself

Eating disorders are multifactorial and require a multidisciplinary team — the S&C professional's job is early recognition and referral.

Chapter 11 — Recap

Nutrition Strategies for Maximizing Performance

✅ Precompetition
Fluid + carb + protein, timed 4h/2h/1h out, always trialed in practice.
✅ Carb Loading
8–10 g/kg/day (10–12 g/kg for marathon) — women need total calories >2,400/day.
✅ During-Event
28–144 g CHO/hr, 6–8% sport drink, <2% body-weight fluid loss.
✅ Postcompetition
1.0–1.85 g CHO/kg/hr + 20–40 g protein within 2 hours.
✅ Performance Goals
Macronutrient targets flex by sport — endurance vs. strength vs. hypertrophy.
✅ Calorie Needs
BMR ~65–70% of TDEE; Cunningham equation accounts for fat-free mass.
✅ Weight Gain
+500 kcal/day, 1.6–2.2 g protein/kg — protein level decides fat vs. lean gain.
✅ Weight Loss
Adherence > diet type. 1.8–2.7 g protein/kg during a ~500 kcal deficit.
✅ RED-S
EA <30 kcal/kg FFM = severe risk; one of the strongest injury-risk predictors.
✅ Eating Disorders
Recognize and refer — never diagnose or treat.
